Sam Nujoma obit

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We examine the legacy of Namibia's first president, Sam Nujoma.

Unique Selling Point:
95 year-old Sam Nujoma was admitted to hospital in late January with some reports describing him as being in critical condition. We examine and recognise his legacy as one of the last members of Southern Africa's liberation movements.

Summary:
Samuel Nujoma was a founding member and the first president of the South West Africa People's Organization (SWAPO) in 1960, campaigning for Namibian independence from South Africa. He established the People's Liberation Army of Namibia (PLAN) in 1962 and led SWAPO during a guerrilla war, the Namibian War of Independence, against the apartheid government from 1966 to 1989. When Namibia achieved independence and held its first democratic elections in 1990, SWAPO won and Nujoma was elected President. He served three terms, and retired as SWAPO president in 2007.

Nujoma has been awarded the Lenin Peace Prize, the Indira Gandhi Peace Prize, and the Ho Chi Minh Peace Prize. The Parliament of Namibia named him "Founding President of the Republic of Namibia" and "Father of the Namibian Nation". In 2007 SWAPO named him "Leader of the Namibian Revolution."

Script:


UPSOUND ARCHIVE: We are the masters of this vast land of our ancestors…
UPSOUND MONDLI MAKHANYA: Nujoma is the last of the generation of liberation heroes.
UPSOUND GREG MILLS:…the man who delivered on the promise of liberation and delivered on the prospects for stability.
UPSOUND ARCHIVE …The destiny of this country is now fully in our hands.
UPSOUND MONDLI MAKHANYA:He was a thinker. He was a fighter and a nation builder.
UPSOUND ARCHIVE:In 1920, the League of Nations gave South Africa a mandate to administer the country, and the seeds of the present controversy were sown.
VOICEOVER: Samuel Shafiishuna Daniel Nujoma was born less than a decade after South Africa took control of what was then South West Africa.
UPSOUND ARCHIVE: Among the domestic measures they’ve brought with them, the policy of apartheid.
VOICEOVER: A four-year genocide under German rule was fresh in the Namibian memory.
UPSOUND MONDLI MAKHANYA: What he had witnessed as a child, what he had witnessed as a young man, as an activist, and as a liberation leader, it had scarred him so deeply. His resentment of Germans was huge. He had this very strong anti-whiteism and anti-Europeanism in him.
VOICEOVER: As South Africa refused to relinquish control, a young Nujoma became increasingly politicised.
UPSOUND ARCHIVE: NUJOMA: It is not the intention of our organisation to fight unnecessarily.
UPSOUND MONDLI MAKHANYA: You grow up as a herd boy. At some point you move to the city. And you are influenced by trade unionism and you see oppression, and then you get involved in liberation politics.
VOICEOVER: In 1960 Nujoma co-founded the South West Africa People’s Organisation, which quickly became the country’s dominant liberation movement. For nearly three decades, he led SWAPO from exile, while its armed wing waged a bitter war of independence.
UPSOUND ARCHIVE: South African casualties are relatively light, but the cost of the war is staggering.
UPSOUND MONDLI MAKHANYA: Nujoma is keeping SWAPO together. He's getting the African continent and the world to see the Namibian struggle against evil.
UPSOUND GREG MILLS: But he also saw the moment of peace for what it was. He saw the opportunity at the end of the 1980s and he seized it with both hands.
UPSOUND ARCHIVE: SWAPO’s leader Sam Nujoma has from exile ordered his fighters to withdraw to Angola.
UPSOUND GREG MILLS: The end of the Cold War provided a brief window of opportunity to negotiate a settlement.
UPSOUND ARCHIVE: QUEEN ELIZABETH Apartheid is dying and South Africa is starting to plan a future in which all its citizens will be equal partners.
UPSOUND GREG MILLS: Nujomo's top achievements undoubtedly are the success of the peace negotiations themselves and the smooth transfer of power.
UPSOUND ARCHIVE: It was shortly after midnight that the South African flag came down to end 75 years of rule by Pretoria.
UPSOUND MONDLI MAKHANYA: His main thing was that, you know what? We are not going to do retribution. And he actually said we are going to nation build. And Namibia to this day is one of the most stable countries on this continent.
UPSOUND ARCHIVE: In 1994, Namibia had its second independent election. SWAPO was voted in again with a convincing two thirds majority.
UPSOUND GREG MILLS: What liberation movements have not been so good at is managing this tension between acquiring control and letting go control. Invariably you end up, uh, embroiling yourself in, in rent and in corruption.
UPSOUND MONDLI MAKHANYA: He was one of the only leaders on the continent who spoke out uncompromisingly in favour of Robert Mugabe.
UPSOUND ARCHIVE: The sanctions against Zimbabwe must be lifted, immediately.
UPSOUND MONDLI MAKHANYA: It made him very, very controversial. You know, at times he couldn't contain himself in his outbursts. But in the actual management of his government, the management of his country, he maintained decorum, he did what he saw as being in the interest of the people of Namibia at the time, not what was just in his head and in his heart.
VOICEOVER: In 1999, Parliament controversially amended the Constitution to allow Nujoma a third term in office.
UPSOUND MONDLI MAKHANYA: What happened with Nujoma was a classic thing of those leaders who feel that they didn't have enough time to do everything that they needed to do. Whereas actually, he had done an amazing job of building a country and creating a stable society that Namibia was.
VOICEOVER: Nujoma formally retired in 2007. His legacy is cemented in history as Father of the Namibian Nation: a model for future generations.
UPSOUND INTERVIEW MONDLI MAKHANYA: Somehow, you know people have a way of separating the icon from the current leadership. Even though he would have planted the seeds for a lot of the wrongs that you see today, people need to believe that there was a purer sense of us.
UPSOUND GREG MILLS: His life's work was really about this transition from an apartheid state to one that was democratic and free and he maintained those standards, and that is a tremendous achievement in itself.
UPSOUND ARCHIVE SAM NUJOM: I move in the name of our people to declare that Namibia is forever free, sovereign and independent. I thank you.
